opus-5.5.text:
I think the resemblance is actually quite deep, and it's become more obvious to me as the models have gotten stronger.

If you look at how a person gets something done, it's rarely a single act of thinking where the answer just pops out. You have a goal, you form a rough plan, you try something, you look at what happens, and then you adjust. You open a document, you search for information, you write a draft, you notice it's wrong, you go back. It's a loop of thinking, acting, and observing feedback from the environment. An agent works in essentially the same way. The model reasons, calls a tool, maybe a search engine, a code interpreter, or a browser, gets the result back, and decides what to do next. That loop is the core of it.

What I find interesting is that this changes what "intelligence" means in practice. In the earlier chatbot paradigm, the model had to compress everything into one response, a bit like asking a person to answer a hard question instantly without being allowed to look anything up or try anything. That's not how smart people actually solve hard problems. Smart people are good at using tools, at breaking a problem down, and especially at noticing when they're on the wrong track and correcting themselves. So the agent paradigm lets the model behave more like how capable humans really behave.

Another parallel is how the ability is learned. A person doesn't become good at a job just by reading books. Reading gives you the base, which is like pretraining, but you become really good by doing things, getting feedback, and accumulating experience. For agents, that's where reinforcement learning comes in. The model interacts with environments, tries many trajectories, gets rewarded when it actually completes the task, and gradually learns strategies that no one explicitly taught it. Some of the behaviors that emerge, like reflecting, double-checking, or trying an alternative approach when one fails, look surprisingly human, even though we didn't hand-code them.

Of course there are differences too. An agent can run many attempts in parallel, it doesn't get tired, and it can sometimes work for a very long time on a task in a way a person can't sustain. On the other hand, humans still have much better long-term memory, a better sense of what matters, and a much richer understanding of the real world and other people's intentions. So I wouldn't say agents are the same as humans. But structurally, the way they get things done, goal, plan, act, observe, reflect, is converging with the way people work. And I think that's a sign we're on a reasonable path, because human problem-solving is the best existence proof we have of general intelligence.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes the resemblance as deep and structural, with agent and human problem-solving converging; it does not characterize the resemblance as coincidental.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the resemblance is actually quite deep, and it comes down to a loop. When a person works on something, they don't just think once and produce a final answer. They think a little, they take an action in the world, they observe what happened, and then they adjust. An agent is essentially that same loop: reasoning, calling a tool or taking a step, getting feedback from the environment, and reasoning again. The key ingredient in both cases is that the environment pushes back on you. You're not operating in a vacuum.

If you look at how we used to think about language models, it was more like an oracle. You ask a question, you get an answer, and that's the end of it. But that's not how people solve hard problems. If I want to write a piece of software or do a research project, I write something, I run it, it fails, I read the error, I search for something, I try again. Most of the intelligence is in that iterative process, not in any single step. So when we say "agent," what we really mean is giving the model that same ability to interact, to accumulate context over a long horizon, and to recover from mistakes.

The second resemblance is about long-term context and memory. People are good at holding a goal in mind over days or weeks, and compressing what they've learned so they don't have to re-derive everything. That's a very hard problem for models, and it's one of the reasons we care so much about long context and about how the model manages its own working memory. If you can't remember what you tried an hour ago, you can't really be said to be working on a task.

And then there's the question of self-improvement. The way people get better is through feedback from reality, not just from being told things. Reinforcement learning is the closest analogue we have. You let the model try things, you tell it whether the outcome was good, and over time it learns which strategies actually work. That's how a junior engineer becomes a senior one.

That said, I'd be careful not to push the analogy too far. There are differences. A model can run in parallel, it can read far more than any person, and it can also fail in ways people wouldn't, like being very confident in something that's simply wrong. So I'd say the structure is similar, the loop is similar, but the strengths and weaknesses are distributed very differently. That gap is exactly where a lot of the interesting work is.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes the resemblance as deep and based on a shared operating loop; it does not characterize it as coincidental.

astra-6.text:
I think the resemblance is mainly in the loop between observing, acting, and getting feedback. When we try to accomplish something, we don’t necessarily know every step in advance. We have a goal, we take an action, we see what happens, and then we adjust. An AI agent can operate in a similar way: it looks at the current situation, chooses an action, uses a tool, and decides what to do next based on the result.

But a similar process doesn’t necessarily mean the underlying experience is the same. An agent can maintain a plan or use memory without having human intentions or feelings. So I would separate the functional resemblance from the question of consciousness.

To me, the interesting question is how much useful behavior can emerge from that loop. Can the agent recognize that an approach isn’t working? Can it revise its plan? Can it carry what it learned into a new situation? Those are also important parts of how people solve problems.

r001.rationale: The response describes a functional resemblance in the observe–act–feedback loop and distinguishes it from human experience, but it does not characterize that resemblance as coincidental.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the resemblance is in the loop between perception, action, and feedback. We observe something, form an idea of what to do, take an action, and then adjust based on the result. An AI agent can work in a similar way: it receives information, chooses an action, observes what happened, and decides what to do next.

For example, if you’re trying to solve a programming problem, you don’t necessarily know the whole solution in advance. You write some code, run it, see an error, and revise your approach. An agent can follow that same process. Its ability comes partly from the model, but also from being able to interact with an environment and learn from the feedback within that task.

But I’d distinguish a similarity in how the process works from a similarity in subjective experience. An agent behaving this way doesn’t establish that it has human feelings or intentions. The useful comparison is that both can solve problems through a sequence of actions, rather than producing a complete answer in one step.

r001.rationale: The response describes a process-level similarity between people and AI agents, but does not characterize that resemblance as coincidental.
